info.title: ouroboros-engine
info.summary: Internal backend for Ouroboros — executes the work ouroboros-rest brokers.
info.description:
The **Python backend** of [Ouroboros](https://github.com/NobuData/ouroboros): the
service that executes the work `ouroboros-rest` brokers.

It is **internal only**. Every request arrives from `ouroboros-rest`, inside the
cluster, carrying a shared secret on the `X-Ouro-Internal-Key` header; a browser
never reaches it. That is a deployment claim, so the service enforces it itself
rather than trusting it — **every path but `/healthz` requires the key**, the
comparison is constant time, and a request without one is refused before routing.

A rejection is therefore one constant body whether the path exists or not: status
codes are how a surface gets mapped from outside, and an unauthenticated caller cannot
tell `/v0/status` from `/v0/anything-else`. Read the `401` documented on each operation
below as the answer to *anything* unauthenticated, including paths this document does
not list.

**Every error has one shape** — `{code, message, details}`, the same envelope
`ouroboros-rest` answers a browser with (`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` § 5.3), so a failure
crossing the gateway does not change form on the way out. `code` is stable and
machine-readable and is what a caller branches on; `message` is written for a person
and is a constant for anything `5xx`, because the real diagnosis names the inside of
this process and belongs in a log; `details` carries what is specific to the failure,
which for a `422` is one entry per field that was refused. That covers the answers no
route produced too — a path nothing claims, a method a path does not allow, a body
that could not be parsed.

`/v0` is the versioned internal prefix. It is unstable by definition — it changes
with the two services that share it, which deploy together — and a stable `/v1` is a
later promise, not this one. A field may be added to a response and a route may be
added to the prefix; a field that disappears, changes type or changes meaning is a
`/v1` served alongside this one, not an edit to it.

servers.description:
`uv run dev`, which binds the loopback interface only. In a deployment the engine
has no public origin at all: it is addressed by its service name from inside the
cluster, and the port comes from `PORT`.

tags.name: service
tags.description: Identity and liveness — what answers before any contract does.

tags.name: v0
tags.description:
The versioned internal contract — what `ouroboros-rest` calls, and the only surface
it mirrors in a typed client
([#35](https://github.com/NobuData/ouroboros/issues/35)). `POST /v0/tasks/echo` is
the exemplar the rest of it is written to: a closed request body, a `422` in the
envelope when it does not validate, and the answering build named in the response.

get.description:
Report that the process is up and serving HTTP.

Deliberately shallow: it opens no connection, reads no configuration and calls
nothing downstream, so it cannot fail for a reason that restarting the container
will not fix. *Readiness* — whether the dependencies a request needs are
reachable — is the REST layer's probe, which asks `/v0/status` with the key.

Report which service and which build is answering. Carries no state, reads no
configuration, and says nothing about health — liveness is `/healthz`.

200.description: The service and its installed version.

get.description:
Answer the two questions that come up when the engine is suspected: *which
version of it is this*, and *is this the same process as a minute ago*.

`ouroboros-rest`'s readiness probe is the intended caller. A `401` here means the
two sides hold different secrets, and REST reports that to a client as a `502` —
never a `401`, because the internal boundary is not something a browser gets to
probe.

200.description: The running build and how long it has been running.

post.description:
Accept a task and hand it straight back. The engine has no real work to do yet —
the task registry, the queue and the worker model are
[#54](https://github.com/NobuData/ouroboros/issues/54) — and this route exists to
settle, with one working round trip, what every later operation would otherwise
settle again: how a request body is described, how it is validated, what a
refusal looks like, and where the version of the answering build is reported.

**The request body is closed.** A property this document does not describe is
refused rather than dropped, so a caller that misspells `payload` is told so
instead of having the field silently ignored.

**The echo is the request.** What comes back under `echo` is the body as the
engine parsed it, so a caller sees what was actually understood rather than what
it believes it sent.

200.description: The task, as received, and the build that received it.

post.summary: Estimate the work in one issue
post.description:
Size one issue: how much work it is, how sure the estimator is, which workflow
should run it, which model it should run on, what the work is expected to cost, and
what any of that was reached from.

**The response is one version of `issue_estimates`**
([#100](https://github.com/NobuData/ouroboros/issues/100)) field for field, so the
caller persists an answer rather than translating one. The five columns with no
field here are the persister's: the row's id, the issue it belongs to, its version,
when it was written, and `trace.sized_at`. An estimator does not know which issue
row it was called for, cannot know which version its answer will become, and must
not be the thing that decides when the answer was written.

**The caller supplies the vocabularies.** `context.workflow_tags` and
`context.model_defaults` are what the installation has, and `suggested_workflow`
and `routed_model` are always drawn from them — roadmap decisions **K5** and
**K6**. This service holds no list of workflow tags and no list of models, so it
cannot invent one; an estimator that names something outside the offer is a `500`
here rather than a value that reaches a row.

**`trace.estimator` is required** — decision **K10**, enforced at this boundary and
not only by the database's `not null`. Provenance checked at the last hop is
provenance the hops before it can lose.

**The estimator behind this contract is replaced and the contract is not.** Today
it is the deterministic rule engine of L.2
([#106](https://github.com/NobuData/ouroboros/issues/106)) — `heuristic-v0`, which
reads an issue's labels, its title and the shape of its body and nothing else. Two
consequences a caller should read from the example below rather than discover:
`breakdown.files` is **always empty**, because a rule engine cannot know which
files an issue touches and an empty list is the honest answer rather than a
missing key; and `trace.tokens_used` is **always `0`**, because nothing was
invoked. `trace.signals` names the rules that produced the answer, so an estimate
can be argued with rather than only accepted. The LLM estimator
([#123](https://github.com/NobuData/ouroboros/issues/123)) answers this same shape,
with the heuristic retained behind it as the fallback path.

**A low confidence is an answer, not a failure.** The heuristic reports how much
its rules agreed; L.3 ([#107](https://github.com/NobuData/ouroboros/issues/107))
compares that against its own floor and moves the issue to `needs_human` rather
than `sized`. The engine publishes the value it is calibrated against —
`ouroboros_engine.estimation.heuristic.NEEDS_HUMAN_CONFIDENCE_FLOOR`, currently
`70` — and the estimate's trace carries a `needs-human:` line when it falls under
it.

**v0 answers synchronously.** A rule engine has nothing to wait for. The
`202`-plus-poll escalation an LLM estimator will need is specified in
`x-async-escalation` below rather than left to be invented then: it adds a status
and a route and changes no field, so a caller written against this operation today
needs only to treat `202` as possible.

x-async-escalation.description:
When an estimator cannot answer inside the caller's deadline, this operation
answers `202` with `{estimation_id, status: "accepted"}` and a `Retry-After`
header. The caller then polls `GET /v0/estimate/{estimation_id}`, which answers
`202` again while the estimate is in flight and **the same `Estimate` body,
unchanged**, when it is done. An estimate that failed is the error envelope on
the poll route, never a `200` carrying half an answer. Adding a status and a
route to `/v0` takes nothing away, so it is compatible with the version rule
rather than a `/v1`.

issue.title: I2C bus lockup after IMU sleep/wake cycle
issue.body:
After entering low-power sleep and waking the BMI270, the I2C bus
intermittently locks up. Recovery requires a full bus reset.

200.description:
The estimate — one version of K.2's row, as the *AI Work Breakdown* panel
renders it.

example.risk_note: M-sized work starts at medium regression risk. heuristic-v0 reads an issue's labels and text only — not the code, its tests, or how much depends on it — so this is where a reviewer starts rather than what the change measures.

signals: workflow: no docs, dependency or feature signal -> standard-fix

InternalKey.name: X-Ouro-Internal-Key
InternalKey.description:
The shared secret both sides of the internal boundary hold: `ouroboros-engine`
reads it from `OURO_ENGINE_SHARED_SECRET`, `ouroboros-rest` sends it. There is no
other credential and no other scheme — no bearer token, no user identity. This
is a service-to-service header, and it is generated per environment.

Unauthorized.description:
The `X-Ouro-Internal-Key` header was missing or wrong. The body is constant: it
names no path, echoes no header and offers no hint about what the key should look
like. What an operator needs is in the engine's log instead, which stays inside
the cluster.

`ouroboros-rest` never forwards this to a browser. A key its own deployment holds
wrongly is its problem and not the caller's, so it logs the mismatch and answers
`502` — never `401`, which would invite a browser to try signing in again against
a boundary it cannot reach at all.

UnprocessableEntity.description:
The request was understood and its content is not acceptable — a missing field, a
`task_kind` that is not a well-formed kind, a property the operation does not
declare. `details` carries one entry per field, keyed the way the caller wrote it,
so each message can be shown against the input that produced it.

`422` rather than `400`: the body parsed, so a caller can tell *I sent the wrong
value* from *I sent something that is not a request*. It is the status
`ouroboros-rest` answers its own validation failures with, and the code is the
same one.

example.message: The request is not valid. See `details` for each field.

status.description:
Always `ok`. A probe reads the status code; this is for the human who runs
the same request by hand.

service.description: Distribution name of this service, constant across deployments.
Distribution name of this service, constant across deployments.

version.description:
Installed version, read from package metadata — the same string `GET /`
reports, so there is one source for "which build is this".

uptime_seconds.description:
Seconds since this process built its application, rounded to milliseconds.
Small and shrinking across calls means something is restarting the container.

EchoRequest.title: EchoRequest
EchoRequest.description:
The body of a `POST /v0/tasks/echo` request, and the shape that comes back under
`echo`. Closed: a property not listed here is refused rather than dropped.

task_kind.description:
Which kind of task this is, as a registry would name it. Lower-case, starting
with a letter, with single `.`, `_` or `-` separators — narrow on purpose,
because this is what a future handler is looked up by and it has to survive
being a dictionary key, a log field and a metric label without quoting.

payload.description:
The task's own arguments. Open, because what a task takes is the task's
business; what the contract requires is that it is an object rather than a
string somebody has to parse twice.

accepted.description:
Always `true`. This route has exactly one success: a request that validates is
accepted, and one that does not is a `422` rather than a `200` carrying
`false`. A task that can be refused while being well-formed is
[#54](https://github.com/NobuData/ouroboros/issues/54)'s, and will say so on a
different route.

echo.description:
The request, as received and after validation — so a caller sees what the
engine actually parsed rather than what it believes it sent.

engine_version.description:
Installed version of the build that answered — the same string `GET /` and
`GET /v0/status` report. In the body rather than only on `/v0/status` because
the gateway logs a round trip it made, and the build that served it belongs in
that line without a second call.

IssueContext.title: IssueContext
IssueContext.description:
The issue being sized, as much of it as an estimator reads. Mirrors K.1's
`github_issues` row ([#99](https://github.com/NobuData/ouroboros/issues/99)) for the
five fields sizing depends on and nothing else from it — an estimator has no
business with `sizing_status` or the row's identifiers, and a field it cannot use is
a field the gateway would have to keep sending.

number.description:
The issue's number within its repository — GitHub's number and the mockup's,
not a database id, so a payload can be read against the page it came from.

title.description: The issue title, as GitHub holds it.
examples: I2C bus lockup after IMU sleep/wake cycle

body.description:
The issue description in full, or `null` for an issue opened without one.
Nullable rather than defaulted to `""` because K.1's column is nullable for the
same reason: GitHub makes no distinction between an empty description and no
description, and this contract does not invent one. Required rather than
optional, so "this issue has no body" is something the caller states rather
than something a missing key implies.
examples: After entering low-power sleep and waking the BMI270, the I2C bus intermittently locks up.

labels.description:
GitHub's label *names*, the way K.1 stores them. The heuristic estimator's
strongest signal, and empty for most issues.

repo.description:
`owner/name` — GitHub's own `full_name`, and what the mockup's head shows. The
pattern is there so a caller that sent only the repository name is refused
rather than having an estimator read an owner out of nothing.

EstimationContext.title: EstimationContext
EstimationContext.description:
The vocabularies that exist, told to the engine rather than assumed by it — roadmap
decisions **K5** and **K6**. A workflow tag and a routed model are opaque strings
this service ascribes no meaning to, and the set of them belongs to the
installation, so the caller sends them and an answer naming anything outside them is
refused before it leaves the engine.

Both are required and non-empty. A request offering no tags has no answer this
contract can give — `suggested_workflow` is required — so it is a `422` rather than
an estimate carrying a field the caller cannot use.

workflow_tags.description:
Every workflow tag the installation has, as the mockup's tag chip shows one.
Opaque, so only their number and length are constrained — a bound is not a
meaning.

model_defaults.description:
The models an estimate may route to, keyed by the caller's own name for the
class of work each is the default for. A map rather than a list because that is
what the caller has, and its *values* are what `routed_model` must be one of.

EstimateRequest.title: EstimateRequest
EstimateRequest.description:
The body of a `POST /v0/estimate` request. Two blocks, and the split is the
contract's argument about who knows what: the issue is the *problem*, and the
context is what the installation happens to be configured with. An estimator reads
both and invents neither. Closed — a property not listed here is refused rather than
dropped.

context.description: The vocabularies an answer may use.

Breakdown.title: Breakdown
Breakdown.description:
The *AI Work Breakdown* panel as data — K.2's `breakdown` jsonb exactly, five keys
and no more. The panel renders four of them; the fifth, `est_minutes`, is what M.3's
queue write reads, which is why it is a stored number rather than something a reader
recomputes from the cycle range.

files.description:
The paths an estimator believes the work touches, as the panel's *Estimated
files touched* list. **Empty is a real answer, and the one `heuristic-v0`
always gives**: a rule engine reading labels and body length cannot know which
files an issue touches, and the mockup renders that absence rather than
guessing. The key is always present — an empty list, never a missing field —
because the two mean different things to a reader. The example below is the
LLM estimator's shape; today's answers carry `[]`.

est_tokens.description:
How many model tokens the *work* is expected to cost. Not what the estimate
cost — that is `trace.tokens_used`, and confusing the two makes a sizing look a
thousand times more expensive than it was.

cycle_min.description: The optimistic end of the wall-clock range, in minutes.

cycle_max.description: The pessimistic end of the wall-clock range, in minutes. Never below `cycle_min`.

est_minutes.description:
The single number the queue plans with, in minutes. Deliberately *not*
constrained to the cycle range: K.2's own example carries a 12–18 minute cycle
beside 23 estimated minutes, because a job's wall clock includes what happens
either side of the model's part of it.

Trace.title: Trace
Trace.description:
Where the estimate came from — K.2's `trace` jsonb, minus its clock. The collapsible
*Estimation trace* under the panel, and the reason re-estimation is auditable at
all: an estimate that cannot say what produced it is one nobody can compare against
the next.

`sized_at` is K.2's and not this contract's. The estimator does not own the clock —
the row's writer does — and a timestamp in a response body is one two services can
disagree about.

estimator.description:
What produced this — `heuristic-v0` for the rule engine installed today, and a
model identifier for the LLM estimator that replaces it. **Decision K10**:
required and non-empty here as well as `not null` there, so provenance cannot be
lost on the way to the row. It is never a model this estimate did not use.

tokens_used.description:
What producing *this estimate* cost, in model tokens. `0` for an estimator that
called no model, which is the honest answer for a rule engine rather than a
missing field — and what `heuristic-v0` always reports.

signals.description:
What the answer was reached from, one line each — a rule name for the heuristic,
a retrieved neighbour for the LLM estimator. Empty rather than absent when an
estimator has nothing to show.

Estimate.title: Estimate
Estimate.description:
The body of a `POST /v0/estimate` response — one version of K.2's `issue_estimates`
row. Every field is a column or a jsonb key of that table; the five columns with no
field here belong to whoever writes the row. Closed, so an estimator cannot smuggle
a field this document does not describe: `/v0` allows a field to be *added* to a
response, and adding one is an edit to this document and to the model together.

effort.description:
How much work this is — the mockup's *Effort* column and K.2's CHECK
constraint, lower case because it is a stored value and a filter key. The
table's `XS` is a presentation decision the UI makes.

confidence.description:
How much the estimator trusts its own answer. The caller reads it against a
floor and routes a low one to `needs_human`, so a hedge is expressed here
rather than by refusing to answer.

suggested_workflow.description:
Which workflow tag should run it — always one of the request's
`context.workflow_tags` (decision **K5**).

routed_model.description:
Which model it should run on — always one of the request's
`context.model_defaults` values (decision **K6**).

risk.description:
How likely the change is to break something — the regression-risk meter's
level, and K.2's other CHECK constraint.

risk_note.description:
The sentence under the meter, saying why. Required and non-empty: a risk level
with no rationale is a colour nobody can argue with, and this is the field a
reviewer reads before overriding an estimate.
examples: Isolated to the I²C driver path; full HIL coverage exists for bus recovery.

trace.description: What produced the estimate, and from what.

Error.title: Error
Error.description:
The shape every error in this service is reported in — the same envelope
`ouroboros-rest` answers a browser with (`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` § 5.3), so a
failure crossing the gateway does not change form on the way out.

code.description:
Stable, machine-readable, and the thing a caller branches on. Derived from the
status rather than invented per call site, so a failure this service has never
answered with still carries an honest code.

message.description:
Written for a person. Never an exception's text and never a stack: anything
`5xx` carries one constant sentence, because the real diagnosis names the
inside of this process and belongs in a log an operator reads.
examples: The request is not valid. See `details` for each field.

details.description:
Whatever is specific to this failure — for a `422`, one entry per field that
was refused, keyed the way the caller wrote it and carrying every message about
it. Empty rather than absent when there is none, so reading `details.task_kind`
never has to check `details` first.
